title: Learning music, early band, wagon and car travel, pay, other bands, dances
summary: Fontenet describes starting music at 17 with friends in New Iberia, touring by wagon then a financed car, early pay, band size and instrumentation, other Southwest Louisiana bands including Bunk Johnson's, and the places and jitney dances they played.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Mr. Fontenet, would you tell us something about your music training when you were a child, something about your music in your home and so on? Well, music training when I was a child, in my home, I started learning music when I was 17 years old. And as I said, with Vanna Band, Adam Broussard, Herbert McPuldoon and I, we were the farmers. We got a Vanna Band and then Tom Edwards, we got Tom Edwards, Robert Stafford, Pete Broussard, Peter Broussard, that's a brother, Adam. Where did your group meet, Mr. Fontenet, at your home or? At Phillip Shaston. Phillip Shaston, he was one of them too. We met at his home. That's where we started. Did you play mostly here in New Iberia? At that time, at that time, yes. For a few years, we, because, well, in fact, we weren't playing, we only tried to learn music. You had a long training here. That's where we started. For a few years, before we started playing. Well, after you got playing, you did some traveling, too. Oh, yes, we did. We, from here to Homewood, Tribido, Donistonville, and west, we, as far as Columbus, Texas. Oh. Johnston, Houston, Houston, we used to be there regularly, from the Port Arthur, Moremont. How did you travel in those days, in the, bus? In the bus. In the bus? Well, but, before we started making those long trips, we used to travel in the wagon. Oh, in the wagon. In the wagon. In the wagon, and then we, we got promoted to a hang. How long did it take you to, uh, to make the wagon trip, Mr. Fontenay? Oh, that is about, I guess about three hours or more. It's been fun trying to play the job after the trip, but then back again, yeah? It's been better, isn't it? No, no, it's better than that. Well, we didn't, we, we didn't, we didn't feel tired. Ha, ha, ha. I guess we were so glad. The beggar of youth. We were so glad to. Tell me, what was the pay in those days for playing Mr. Fontenay? Well, when I, when I first started playing the Don La Quarter piece. Don La Quarter piece. And you'd go over and wipe it for that. Well, no, we, we, that was around here, we would get full. Uh-huh. But, two dollars and a half. It was after the war, the royal war, he wasn't there. He went up on that price. Uh, how many men were there in this first combo? Seven. And what was the most number of men that you had in the other combos that you played with? I noticed you have ten in the banner band there. Is that the most that you ever had? Yeah. That's the most. What the number of men do you like most or did you prefer most in your general, your combo? Well, it was, when we, we had the, ten it was easier than when we had seven. Uh-huh. Now what was the usual, uh, instrumentation you had there? I think three brass, two trumpets and a trombone, and what, what else did you have there? Three, uh, they had the, three saxes, three saxes, uh-huh. And they doubled on anything? Yeah. Yeah. One of the saxes, he was, he was, uh, he was, uh, double on the bass, drums. Uh-huh. He could get down also. Uh-huh. He played. Mr. Pondett, you were talking a while ago about riding the Lafayette in a wagon. When did you fellas get your first car? Well, after we stopped traveling in the wagon, we used to rent automobiles to carriers. They charged so much, we thought of buying an automobile of our own. And, uh, Mr. Harry Hall and Mr. Amy Vittery, they were automobile dealers. He spoke to them about financing us to get by a second-handed. They said, if they wouldn't, they had a Dodge. They had a Dodge truck bag, a caja around. They would sell it to us. Uh, if we could put up a certain amount of money. We were doing so well at that time. They lent it to us. We were going for four days. They lent it to us for the four days with understanding that what we would pay someone else for an automobile, that we would put that on a down payment. And our first down payment was $136 to them. After that, every week we would give $25 every Sunday. We were playing in Youngville. And we'd have any games we'd have during the week where we would pay so much. The first month we had this car, we paid them $482. $137. How much was the total cost of the automobile? It was $1300. And that was the second hand? No, it was the second hand. Oh, I see, I see. And the second month we paid $372. Oh, you were kind of bringing that debt down in a hurry. When did they pay back some of the interest? Very much, three, seven, six. They were very nice with us. They got a mind and charge us any interest. They didn't charge any interest? Well, Mr. Hall, he knew me and Robert Stafford very well. And that's the way we got the... He said afterwards, they'd give us this good service, it helped them to sell other cars. They made money by letting us have them. Would you tell us about some of the other bands in this area in Southwest Louisiana that you knew about? Well, you see, they had the Black Eagle and Crowley, and they had the Yelping Hound. He was playing with the Yelping Hound. The Yelping Hound. Where were they from? They were from Crowley. Crowley. Then... What about the V-Doll band? Well, that was more on the other day. A Coyson music? It wasn't Coyson, it was all brass on. Oh? What band was this? V-Doll band. V-Doll band. That's... They didn't play jazz or ragtime music. They had Gabriel from Timidoo. They had... Clever Williams from Donison. No, no, no. It was Stood from Baton Rouge. Tooth Johnson. What was the one from Baton Rouge? Stood and... And Tooth Johnson. Was he a trumpet player? Tooth Johnson. Yeah, what did Tooth Johnson play? Nothing. I think it was his brother. Victor. Yeah. He played violin, I think. Tooth Johnson was from Baton Rouge. Yes. And they had the Royal Band in Lake Charlottes. How big were these bands? Most of them? Well, most of the bands at that time were seven or eight. Did they play a bar like the band? You felt they were better than they were? Naturally. He felt we were better than all of them. And in many instances, it was a problem. It was true. Well, when you had Bunk Johnson in your band, you probably felt y'all had the best band of them all, huh? Well, I'm a mauler. He did a... He did something hard to beat. Do you know of any outstanding musicians from these other groups that finally got the fame that Bunk got? What about Lawrence Dewey? Was he fairly well known? Well, he was. He was in his family. He didn't get the fame that Bunk. No, he didn't. What was the fame that he had in Bunk? Well, he didn't get the fame that Bunk. Which one is that? That's the trumpet player that I tell you about that could play his fame. Oh, yeah. What was his name again? E-Van Thomas. Oh, yeah. Mr. Farnett, what was, what were some of the places you played in this area? Would you tell us something about the dances that you played for? Sure. Well, Sheraton Beach, one of the places we played there Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sunday. Every other Sunday. Every other Sunday. Every other Sunday. And we played in Youngville every other Sunday. Played Appleville, Erath, Gaydon, Kaplan, Eunice, Opelousa, Generate, Morgan City, Franklin. Homer, Thibodeau, Donaldsonville, Nick Chung, Crowley, Bill Platt. Gee, that was quite a wide area. Would you tell us something about the dances? How did, were there just regular dances? Well, it was, it was regular dances. In, in, uh, Sheraton, well, they had what they, they called a jitney dances. Uh-huh. You would play a number, and then everybody would leave off the pavilion. And as soon as they'd play off the pavilion, you'd start another. Uh-huh. And they'd charge them ten cents a day. Ten cents a day, sir. And they'd charge the gentleman ten cents a day. That was the only place that had that? Well, at Lafayette, once there was a fair, and they had a jitney dance. So, we played another time in Crowley, Franklin. Uh-huh. They had, but most of the dances were regular dances. Well, you certainly did quite a bit of traveling. Play all these dances, all these tongues. Well, at that time, they didn't have, they didn't have these nightclubs. Yeah. We were playing every night. Uh-huh. But today, with all these nightclubs, everybody dancing on Saturday.
